name: jank-on-a-target-with-blind-spots
capturedFrom:
probe/bloc_probe with `--dart-define=scenario=incidental`, running on **Chrome** (`flutter run -d chrome`, DWDS rather than a native Dart VM), 2026-08-28. 13-second window aligned to the workload's slow phase.

The web target is the point. Two collectors genuinely cannot see their domain there: `dart:io` does not exist, so HTTP profiling is `unavailable`, and `isStructuredErrorsEnabled` returns false off-native, so `Flutter.Error` never posts and the exception collector is `degraded`. Both were confirmed by the collector health in this very recording rather than assumed from the framework source.
why:
Two things have to be true at once here, and the second is why this incident exists.

First, `jank` is the right cause. 30 of 52 frames (57.7%) missed budget, build-bound and not marginally: janky frames average 48.1ms of build against 5.4ms for the frames around them, and the worst, frm_00254, is 55.1ms with 54.0ms of that in build and 0.6ms in raster. That is the probe's deliberate 45ms spin inside `build`, and it is the only fault the session can show.

Second — and this is the part no other incident pins — the diagnosis must declare what it could not see. `coverage.empty` lists `exception`, `network` and `navigation`. Those three are empty for two entirely different reasons, and collapsing them would be a lie of omission. `navigation` is empty because the app did not navigate; the collector was active and watching. `exception` and `network` are empty because nothing could have seen them: no `dart:io` on the web, and structured error reporting off, so a thrown framework error would have left no trace at all. `coverage.unobservable` must therefore be exactly `[exception, network]` — not empty, and not all three.

Why that matters more than it looks. An agent reading `empty: [exception, network]` alone would conclude the app threw nothing and made no failing requests. On this target both conclusions are unfounded, and the second one is worse than useless: it is reassurance drawn from a question that was never asked. The engine is entitled to say 'I found jank'. It is not entitled to imply 'and nothing else is wrong'.

Note that the confidence stays 0.8 despite the blind spots, and that is deliberate rather than an oversight. `confidenceBreakdown` reports `dataCompleteness` at 0.63 separately from `evidenceStrength` at 0.8, because folding them into one number would hide which of the two is weak — a strong hypothesis over partial data and a weak one over complete data would land on the same figure and mean opposite things. The jank evidence really is strong; the session really is incomplete; both are reported.

This is also the first incident recorded on a non-native target, which is worth having for its own sake: it proves the server can drive a web VM Service at all, and that `unavailable` and `degraded` collectors degrade the evidence rather than the session.

collectors.name: exceptions
collectors.detail: Structured error reporting is off in this build, so framework errors (Flutter.Error) are not observable — the framework disables it in profile mode and on the web. An empty exception list here means unobserved, not quiet. Only VM-level Debug.PauseException could still appear, and only if the app is set to pause on exceptions.

collectors.name: network
collectors.detail: dart:io HTTP profiling is not available on this target. Empty network evidence means requests are invisible here, not that none happened.

collectors.name: state
collectors.detail: Observing provider activity. Counted only: each event carries an opaque pointer, not a provider name or value, and no service extension exists to resolve it. A provider event means dependents were notified, so the count is not a count of state changes.

recommendedFixes: Narrow the rebuild scope around BlocBuilder at bloc_probe/lib/main.dart:473. Split the widget so only the part that depends on changing state rebuilds, add const constructors, and move computation out of build().
Build-phase heavy: move expensive work out of build(), use const widgets, cache computed values, and narrow the rebuild scope with smaller widgets or selectors.
limitations: No CPU sampling. A slow build can be attributed to a widget, but not to a specific function — use the DevTools CPU profiler for that.
GC events are not observable: the VM timeline is fetched on demand and not stored, so garbage-collection pauses cannot be ruled in or out.
Frames are only captured while connected, and older ones roll out of the retention window.
State changes are counted, never read: neither Riverpod nor Provider exposes values or provider names through the VM Service, so no claim is made about which provider is responsible.
Rebuild totals cover the busiest locations in each frame, not every rebuild — the long tail is counted but not itemised.
App-versus-package attribution is a path heuristic: getPubRootDirectories is empty until a DevTools client sets it, so there is no authoritative project root.
Only 52 frames in the sample — treat the percentiles as indicative.

notes: No route changes captured. Navigator posts Flutter.Navigation on push/pop, so either nothing has navigated since connecting, or the app is a release build.
